questions.question: Define gravity and state two factors that affect the size of the gravitational force between two objects. What happens to the force when the distance is doubled? Explain why an astronaut weighs less on the Moon.
questions.expected_answer: Gravity is a force of attraction between any two objects that have mass. The force is larger when the masses are larger and smaller when the distance between them is larger. Doubling the distance reduces the force to a quarter (inverse square). Weight is the pull of gravity on a mass; the Moon has much less mass than Earth, so its gravity at its surface is about one sixth of Earth's, and the astronaut (same mass) weighs about one sixth as much.

questions.question: Use Newton's cannon to explain how an object stays in orbit. Explain what would happen to the Earth if the Sun's gravity disappeared, and why astronauts in the International Space Station float.
questions.expected_answer: A cannonball fired horizontally from a high mountain curves down to the ground; fired faster, it lands further away. At about 8 km/s the Earth's surface curves away beneath it as fast as it falls, so it keeps falling but never reaches the ground and travels round the Earth: it is in orbit. An orbit is a balance between gravity pulling the object towards the centre and its sideways speed carrying it forward. If the Sun's gravity disappeared, the Earth would move off in a straight line in the direction it was travelling. Astronauts float because they and the station are falling around the Earth together; gravity there is still about 90% of that on the ground.

questions.question: Explain how the distance of a planet from the Sun affects its orbital speed and period, using two examples. Explain why the Solar System is disc-shaped.
questions.expected_answer: Closer to the Sun, gravity is stronger, so a planet must move faster to stay in orbit, and it has a shorter path; so inner planets have shorter periods. Examples: Mercury about 47 km/s, year 88 days; Earth about 30 km/s, 365¼ days; Neptune about 5.4 km/s, about 165 years. The Solar System formed from a cloud of gas and dust that collapsed under gravity; it was slowly rotating, and as it collapsed it spun faster (like a skater pulling in her arms). Spin resisted collapse around the axis but not along it, so the cloud flattened into a spinning disc with the Sun forming at the centre; the planets formed in the disc, so they orbit in nearly the same plane and the same direction.
